    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">Matariki is the Māori New Year. It begins when the Matariki star cluster rises in the early morning sky in mid-winter. 

This year’s theme is Matariki herenga waka – Matariki is a mooring place for all canoes. It highlights inclusion and belonging for everyone in Aotearoa New Zealand. 

Today, Matariki is celebrated across the country, with many people taking part by learning about its meaning, sharing kai (food), telling stories, and spending time together. 

There are many events that bring people together to celebrate Matariki and the diversity of our communities. You can find events near you and how to take part by visiting <a class="link" href="https://www.matariki.com/?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" rel="nofollow" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>https://www.matariki.com/</a>. 

Keen to know what Matariki means in your own language? This year, the Matariki principles have been translated into a range of ethnic languages commonly spoken in New Zealand, including Afrikaans, Chinese (Traditional and Simplified), French, Hindi, Spanish, and Tagalog. 
•	Multilingual Matariki Principles (web version): <a class="link" href="https://bit.ly/4goJ4Bh?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" rel="nofollow" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>https://bit.ly/4goJ4Bh</a>

Mānawatia a Matariki (celebrate Matariki).</p>

    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">We are pleased to announce the appointment of Pratima Namasivayam as Chief Executive of the Ministry for Ethnic Communities, for one year from 1 July 2026. 

Many will already know Pratima as a senior public leader with experience across a range of sectors, such as National Security, Emergency, Justice and Central agencies. Across these settings, she has led cross-system work in highly visible operating conditions to deliver meaningful results for communities across Aotearoa New Zealand. 

Since joining the Ministry in 2022, Pratima has shaped how government understands and responds to Ethnic Communities. This includes strengthening the availability of data evidence and increasing support on security and resilience issues, to name a few. 

More information about these initiatives is available on our website: 
👉️ <a class="link" href="https://lnkd.in/gKN67KCV?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" rel="nofollow" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>https://lnkd.in/gKN67KCV</a>  
👉️ <a class="link" href="https://lnkd.in/eCpuYiwp?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" rel="nofollow" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>https://lnkd.in/eCpuYiwp</a> 

We look forward to her leading the Ministry into its next chapter. This means continuing to use evidence, listening to communities, and working across government to improve outcomes. It also means recognising the important contribution Ethnic Communities make to New Zealand's resilience and prosperity.</p>

    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">Celebrated annually on 25 May, Africa Day is an annual commemoration of African unity and heritage. Communities gathered at The Base Spaces in Wynyard Quarter on Saturday 23 May to celebrate the occasion in Auckland for the fifth consecutive year. The day began with a pōwhiri (formal welcome), led by Tangata whenua kaumātua alongside African community leaders. It set the tone for a vibrant programme featuring cultural food, arts, crafts, information stalls, and performances by African artists and other cultures.

Our Engagement Specialist, <a class="link" href="https://nz.linkedin.com/in/fungai-mhlanga-9ab0a35b?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>Fungai Mhlanga</a>, attended the celebration in Auckland and spent time connecting with community leaders, stallholders and whānau. 

We acknowledge the African Communities Forum Incorporated (ACOFI) Acting President Adekemi Àjàyí and the Executive Committee, the Africa Day 2026 Organising Committee, community leaders, and volunteers whose efforts made the celebration possible.

    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">There is no single pathway into governance, but there are practical steps people can take to prepare for board opportunities!

We recently completed in person governance sessions in Auckland and Christchurch, and an online session for Wellington. These sessions aimed to support people from Ethnic Communities to better understand the requirements for public sector and Crown board roles. They are delivered as part of the Ministry’s Nominations Service. 

Speakers shared their governance journeys, practical insights, and honest advice about what it takes to serve on public sector boards. Building governance capability, gaining relevant experience, and remaining persistent and patient are all important. A key message across all sessions was that there is no single pathway into governance. Building governance capability, gaining relevant experience, and remaining persistent and patient are all important, particularly given the high level of competition for public sector board appointments.

        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">More than 130 students from across Aotearoa New Zealand took part in the 2026 Race Unity Speech Awards, sharing thoughtful ideas about identity, belonging and inclusion.

We have supported the Awards since 2009, helping create space for young people to share their voices, experiences and ideas.

    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">Today we acknowledge the Ascension of Bahá’u’lláh - a sacred observance for members of the Bahá’í community that marks the passing of Bahá’u’lláh, the founder of the Bahá’í Faith, on 29 May 1892. 

The day is observed through prayer, quiet reflection, and devotional readings. Many Bahá’í communities gather in the early hours of the morning commemorate Bahá’u’lláh’s passing.

In Aotearoa New Zealand, the Bahá’í community has made long-standing contributions to social cohesion and inclusion, including efforts to counter racism through establishing the first Race Unity Speech Award, and its work with the @Hedi Moani Charitable Trust.

At the Ministry for Ethnic Communities, we acknowledge important cultural and faith observances alongside the contributions Ethnic Communities make to a more inclusive Aotearoa. </p>
